rv.q: His script crackles with sweetness and freshness
This new version of 'Cinderella' is a sleek, funny and surprisingly feminist take on the classic fairy tale that should please both kids and their parents.

This new version of the musical, which opened Sunday night at the Broadway Theater, turns out to be a satisfying piece of old-fashioned musical theater that has been given just enough contemporary touches to feel fresh without losing its essential sweetness.

Rodgers & Hammerstein’s (and Beane’s and Brokaw’s) Cinderella is as solidly entertaining a commercial proposition as they come, featuring one of Broadway’s finest ensembles and what might be its couple of the year:

But this pleasurable confection overcomes its conceptual missteps with old-fashioned stagecraft, enchanting design elements, smooth direction and choreography, and most of all, winning contributions from an ideally cast ensemble.
Laura Osnes makes a lovely Cinderella, with a crystalline soprano that gives the familiar songs a fresh sparkle

Miraculously, this is the 'Rodgers & Hammerstein Cinderella' the American musical theatre has been waiting for.

But with guidance from director Mark Brokaw and librettist Douglas Carter Beane, Osnes and a gifted supporting cast make this fairy tale very much their own -- a scrumptious trifle that, for all its hokey moments, will charm theatergoers of all ages.
This new Broadway production of Rodgers + Hammerstein's Cinderella is a sumptuous, family-friendly spectacle that succeeds in bringing fresh life to the beloved musical.
Luckily, there are some fairy godmothers behind the scenes who redeem this production.
The result is an unwieldy but crowd pleasing concoction that ends up being reasonably entertaining despite its jarring multiple tones.

You can see light beaming from Laura Osnes at the Broadway Theatre, where she's playing the Cinderella of any girl's fantasy.Last seen in a flop called "Bonnie and Clyde," Osnes has doe-eyed charm, a lovely soprano and whatever it is that separates a star from the chorus without trumpeting the fact.
The rest of the cast–theater pros–deliver, of course.
